claims.text: The initial non-equilibrium alloy contains primary solid-solution regions together with metastable intermetallic compounds.
Post-solidification thermal activation drives elemental diffusion in the alloy.
Thermal aging causes Mg to segregate from the primary solid solution.
Segregated Mg forms fine-scale Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates at grain boundaries and near-surface regions.
Mg segregation produces compositional gradients at grain boundaries and near-surface regions.
The segregation-associated compositional gradients modify the structure of the resulting oxide scale.
Mg redistribution locally depletes Al or Cu that would otherwise be available for protective-film formation.
Al or Cu aids formation of a coherent, protective oxide film in the proposed alloy system.
The altered surface composition promotes formation of MgO or a mixed Mg-containing oxide scale.
The MgO or mixed-oxide scale is more porous and less adherent than the oxide scale on the as-cast state.
The more porous and less-adherent oxide scale is less protective.
Thermally aged material will have a faster corrosion rate than the as-cast baseline, including a higher corrosion current density.
Thermally aged material will form a thicker oxide scale during high-temperature oxidation than the as-cast baseline.
The aged alloy's oxide scale will be more porous and less adherent, causing accelerated high-temperature degradation.
The as-cast baseline lacks significant Mg segregation and precipitate-induced depletion of protective elements.
The as-cast baseline has superior corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the thermally aged state.
The proposed mechanism is limited to alloys with density below 6 g/cm³.
The proposed mechanism requires a non-equilibrium initial state in which elemental partitioning is kinetically limited.
Thermal treatment at approximately 300–500 °C can drive the proposed transformation without complete melting.
The kinetics and extent of segregation and the resulting performance changes depend on alloy composition and thermal history.
